The test image shows a corn ear with:
- Exposed kernels (husks gone or fallen)
- Orange/tan kernels with heavy dark/black material throughout
- White-gray mass at the top of the ear
- Significant darkening/blackening of the cob tissue

Top candidates: Diplodia_Ear_Rot, Gibberella_Disease, Common_Smut, Fusarium_Disease. Let me view references.
Common Smut 218 is very similar — white/gray gall at top turning black, kernels still visible. Continuing to cover more classes before confirming.

Head Smut (tassel), Trichoderma (green mold), Tar Spot (leaf spots), Northern Leaf Blight (leaf lesions), Gray Leaf Spot (field defoliation), and Common Rust (leaf pustules) are all clearly different from the test image.

**Summary of evidence:**

The test image shows an ear on a green-background plant with:
- Orange/tan kernels still partially intact
- Heavy black material throughout (mature smut teliospores)
- White/gray bulging mass at the ear tip (immature smut gall not yet ruptured)

**Common Smut reference 218** matches almost exactly: white/gray galls at the top transitioning to black, with normal kernels still visible alongside infected tissue. This is the classic Common Smut progression — galls start white/silvery and rupture to release black teliospores.

All ear rot candidates (Diplodia, Gibberella, Fusarium, Aspergillus, Trichoderma) were ruled out: none produce this white-gall-plus-black-spore-mass pattern. Head Smut affects the tassel, not the ear in this manner.
